milkweed.origin: Milkweed floss is the seed hair (coma) of milkweeds, chiefly common milkweed, Asclepias syriaca (Apocynaceae), native to eastern North America. It is cultivated in Quebec, Canada, where researchers note that it needs no irrigation, pesticides or fertilizers. The name milkweed is also applied to seed floss of the separate genus Calotropis, including Calotropis procera and Calotropis gigantea (also Apocynaceae), called giant milkweed, which grow in arid regions of Asia and Africa and are invasive in some countries.
milkweed.structure: Each floss fiber is a single seed-hair cell, a thin-walled hollow tube whose empty channel has been measured at more than 90 percent of fiber volume, with intra-fiber porosity of about 0.83. Composition reported for Canadian milkweed is roughly 40 to 45 percent cellulose, 35 to 40 percent hemicellulose, 15 percent lignin, 3 percent free sugars and 3 percent wax. The wax makes the surface strongly hydrophobic, with water contact angles around 140 degrees, while the thin walls make fibers fragile and prone to collapse under pressure.
milkweed.process: Mature pods are collected and the floss is separated from the seeds. Because the fibers are short, smooth, brittle and low in cohesion, they card poorly: studies report that air-laying gives an overall yield of about 90 percent, far better than carding. Floss is therefore blended with binder fibers such as low-melt polyester or polylactic acid, air-laid into webs and thermally bonded, or developed into insulating fillings for winter jackets and building insulation.
milkweed.performance: Milkweed is valued for insulation, buoyancy and oil sorption rather than strength. Air-laid nonwovens containing 30 to 70 percent milkweed showed thermal conductivity of about 28 to 35 mW/m K at densities of only 11 to 19 kg/m3, lower than a commercial hemp insulation tested alongside, and good sound absorption. Superhydrophobic floss has absorbed up to about 100 g of oil per g. Weaknesses include fragility in carding, collapse of hollow fibers under high molding pressure, and flammability like other cellulosics.
milkweed.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: milkweed floss burns quickly like other light cellulosic floss. Microscopy shows smooth, straight, thin-walled hollow tubes without cotton's convolutions, very similar to kapok, so the two are hard to separate visually; seed source documentation and careful measurement of diameter and wall thickness help. Fills sold as milkweed may be blends with synthetic fibers, and FTIR or solubility tests can detect polyester.
milkweed.labeling: Milkweed is not among the Annex I fibre names in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, so EU labels would generally show it as other fibres with its percentage. In the US, covered textile products disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303, using the common name for natural fibers; blends with polyester or PLA binder fibers must name those generics. Fill and bedding products may be subject to additional rules, and pollinator or habitat claims should be substantiated.
milkweed.past: Milkweed floss has long been compared with kapok as a buoyant, insulating fill. Accounts of wartime pod-collection campaigns in North America to replace scarce kapok are widely repeated but were not verified against primary sources in this pass. Recent Canadian research has turned Quebec-grown milkweed into jacket fillings, building insulation and bio-composites for automobile dashboards, while Indian and Iranian studies have tested Asclepias and Calotropis floss as oil sorbents and filters.

henequen.origin: Henequen is the leaf fiber of Agave fourcroydes (Asparagaceae), native to Mexico and Guatemala and domesticated on the Yucatan Peninsula from the wild Agave angustifolia. Yucatan remains the historic center of cultivation, where research centers such as the Centro de Investigacion Cientifica de Yucatan study its biology and byproducts. The leaf juice, rich in fructans, and henequen mezcal are coproducts, and the fiber is also called Mexican sisal in trade.
henequen.structure: Like sisal, henequen technical fibers are bundles of lignified cellulosic cells with lumens, embedded in leaf parenchyma and extracted as long strands. Recent characterization describes extra-long staple length, adequate bundle strength and thermal stability up to about 220 C. Henequen is generally described as coarser than sisal. Cultivated cordage varieties show domestication traits including larger size, higher fiber content, fewer spines and reduced reproductive capacity compared with wild populations.
henequen.process: Mature leaves are cut from the long-lived plants, then decorticated mechanically: rotating scrapers remove pulp and cuticle while water washes the fiber; the fructan-rich leaf juice released in this step has been studied as a fermentation feedstock for ethanol. Fibers are dried in the sun, brushed, graded and baled, then spun into binder twine and rope, woven into rugs, or used in crafts. Studies also extract fiber by water retting followed by mechanical separation. Plants are propagated clonally, and micropropagation methods have been developed because breeding by seed is difficult.
henequen.performance: Henequen is strong, stiff and coarse, with properties broadly comparable to sisal but a harsher hand; Britannica notes it is coarser and less attractive than sisal and suited above all to agricultural binder twine. It is hydrophilic and swells when wet, like other leaf fibers. Thermal stability to about 220 C permits normal textile processing. It dyes like other cellulosics with direct and reactive dyes.
henequen.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: henequen burns like other cellulosic leaf fibers. It is very hard to distinguish from sisal by eye or simple microscopy, since both are agave leaf fibers with similar bundles; species-level identification may need anatomical study or DNA markers. Isozyme studies have shown that each cultivar is genetically uniform, a result of clonal propagation. Plastic twines imitating natural fiber melt rather than char.
henequen.labeling: Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists henequen (Agave fourcroydes) as an Annex I fibre name separate from sisal (Agave sisalana) and maguey (Agave cantala), so EU labels should use the correct agave name. In the US, covered textiles must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303, naming natural fibers by common name; calling henequen sisal would misidentify the species. Twine and cordage may fall outside apparel labeling rules.
henequen.past: Botanical evidence suggests that the ancient Maya domesticated henequen from wild Agave angustifolia in Yucatan, selecting lines for cordage and finer textile fiber. The late nineteenth and early twentieth century henequen boom in Yucatan, driven by demand for binder twine, rested on large haciendas and Maya labor under conditions historians describe as coercive, including debt servitude; this pass did not verify specific figures, so readers should consult historical scholarship. Promotion of a single cordage cultivar through clonal propagation since the mid-twentieth century left the crop genetically narrow, and the finer textile cultivar Kitam Ki is nearly extinct.
